Course Overview
ECO 112 introduces you to macroeconomics: the study of modern economies at a national level. We’ll focus on national income accounts, monetary and fiscal policy, and economic growth. By the end of the course, you should be able to apply these concepts to analyze national economies, engage in policy debates, and follow international economic events with real understanding.

title: Chapter 13: Fiscal Policy, Deficits, and Debt
text:
To fight a recession, should the government use expansionary or contractionary fiscal policy? Name two specific tools it could use.
To fight demand-pull inflation, should the government use expansionary or contractionary fiscal policy?
True or False: automatic stabilizers require Congress to pass new legislation every time the economy changes.
As GDP rises in an expansion, what automatically happens to tax revenue and to transfer payments, without any new laws being passed?
A country’s actual budget shows a deficit this year, but its cyclically adjusted budget is balanced. What does this combination suggest about whether the deficit was caused by fiscal policy choices or by the state of the economy?
What is the difference between refinancing the public debt and retiring it?
Why might economists consider debt as a percentage of GDP more meaningful than the absolute dollar amount of debt?



Show Answer


Expansionary. Increase government spending (G), decrease taxes (T), or both.
Contractionary. Decrease G, increase T, or both.
False. Automatic stabilizers work without any new legislation, that is exactly what makes them “automatic.”
Tax revenue rises automatically (more income pushes people into higher tax brackets under a progressive system) and transfer payments fall automatically (fewer people qualify for unemployment benefits, for example).
It suggests the deficit was caused mainly by the economy being below full employment (automatic stabilizers responding to a weak economy), not by a deliberately expansionary fiscal policy choice, since at full employment the budget would be balanced under current law.
Refinancing means rolling over the debt, selling new bonds to pay off maturing ones. Retiring means actually paying the debt off, buying back bonds or letting them mature without replacing them.
Debt as a percentage of GDP accounts for the size of the economy that has to service the debt, a large absolute debt is a much smaller burden for a large, wealthy economy than for a small one, so comparing the percentage is more meaningful across time or across countries.

title: Chapter 13: Fiscal Policy, Deficits, and Debt
text:
Problem 1: Closing a Recessionary Gap
An economy has a recessionary expenditure gap of $100 billion (aggregate expenditures at full-employment GDP fall $100 billion short of what is needed). The MPC in this economy is 0.8.

What is the multiplier?
How large an increase in government spending (G) alone would close this gap?
How large a tax cut (T) alone would close this gap? (Recall a tax change’s effect is multiplied by MPC first, then by the multiplier.)
Propose one combination of a smaller increase in G together with a tax cut that, added together, would also close the gap exactly.



Show Answer


Multiplier \(= 1/(1-0.8) = 5\).
\(\Delta G\) needed: \(100 / 5 = \$20\) billion.
\(\Delta T\) needed: \(100 / (5 \times 0.8) = \$25\) billion tax cut.
Many combinations work, for example: a \(\$10\) billion increase in G (closes \(10 \times 5 = \$50\) billion of the gap) plus a \(\$12.5\) billion tax cut (closes \(12.5 \times 0.8 \times 5 = \$50\) billion of the gap), together closing the full $100 billion gap. Any pair of G and T changes that add up to $100 billion in combined AD effect works.

title: Chapter 13: Fiscal Policy, Deficits, and Debt
text:
Problem 2: The Balanced-Budget Multiplier
The government increases spending by $30 billion and, in the same year, raises taxes by exactly $30 billion to keep the budget balanced. The MPC is 0.8.

Using the multiplier, what is the effect of the $30 billion increase in G alone on equilibrium GDP?
Using the tax multiplier (\(MPC \times\) multiplier), what is the effect of the $30 billion increase in T alone on equilibrium GDP?
Combining (a) and (b), what is the net effect on equilibrium GDP?
Explain in one sentence why an equal-sized increase in G and T does not fully cancel out, even though the government’s budget balance does not change at all.



Show Answer


\(\Delta GDP\) from G: \(30 \times 5 = +\$150\) billion.
\(\Delta GDP\) from T: \(-30 \times 0.8 \times 5 = -\$120\) billion.
Net effect: \(150 - 120 = +\$30\) billion, equilibrium GDP rises by exactly the size of the balanced budget change itself. This is the balanced-budget multiplier: it always equals 1.
Every dollar of new government spending enters the economy in full, but a dollar of new taxes only reduces spending by \(MPC\) of a dollar (households absorb the rest by saving less), so the spending increase always outweighs the tax increase’s contractionary effect.

title: Chapter 13: Fiscal Policy, Deficits, and Debt
section: Problem 3: Automatic Stabilizers, Progressive vs. Flat Taxes
text:
Problem 3: Automatic Stabilizers, Progressive vs. Flat Taxes
Compare two hypothetical tax systems facing the same household, whose income falls from $60,000 to $50,000 during a downturn:

System A (progressive): 10 percent on the first $40,000 of income, 25 percent on income above $40,000.
System B (flat): 18 percent on all income, regardless of amount.


Compute this household’s tax bill under System A at $60,000 income and at $50,000 income.
Compute the tax bill under System B at both income levels.
Under which system does the tax bill fall by more when income drops?
Compute disposable (after-tax) income under each system at both income levels, and the drop in disposable income under each. Which system cushions the household’s spending power more?



Show Answer



                            
                                            



At $60,000: \(10\% \times 40{,}000 + 25\% \times 20{,}000 = 4{,}000 + 5{,}000 = \$9{,}000\). At $50,000: \(4{,}000 + 25\% \times 10{,}000 = 4{,}000 + 2{,}500 = \$6{,}500\).
At $60,000: \(18\% \times 60{,}000 = \$10{,}800\). At $50,000: \(18\% \times 50{,}000 = \$9{,}000\).
System A’s tax bill falls by \(9{,}000 - 6{,}500 = \$2{,}500\). System B’s falls by only \(10{,}800 - 9{,}000 = \$1{,}800\). The progressive system’s tax revenue falls by more.
Disposable income, System A: \(60{,}000-9{,}000=\$51{,}000\) then \(50{,}000-6{,}500=\$43{,}500\), a drop of $7,500. System B: \(60{,}000-10{,}800=\$49{,}200\) then \(50{,}000-9{,}000=\$41{,}000\), a drop of $8,200. The progressive system (A) cushions the household’s spending power more, its disposable income falls by less, exactly the automatic-stabilizer effect at work.

title: Chapter 13: Fiscal Policy, Deficits, and Debt
text:
Problem 4: Accumulating the Public Debt
A small country starts with zero public debt in Year 1. It then runs a deficit of $45 billion in Year 2, a surplus of $10 billion in Year 3, and a deficit of $20 billion in Year 4.

What is the country’s public debt at the end of Year 4?
If this country’s real GDP in Year 4 is $550 billion, what is its public debt as a percentage of GDP?
Suppose most of this debt is held by the country’s own citizens and financial institutions (internally held) rather than by foreign lenders. Briefly explain why economists generally consider this less burdensome than the same debt held externally.
Name one way that financing this debt could crowd out private investment, connecting back to the market for loanable funds from Chapter 6.



Show Answer


Debt accumulates deficits minus surpluses: \(45 - 10 + 20 = \$55\) billion.
\(55 / 550 \times 100 = 10\) percent of GDP.
When debt is held internally, paying interest or principal mostly just transfers purchasing power from one group of the country’s own residents (taxpayers) to another (bondholders), the money stays within the domestic economy. Externally held debt sends that purchasing power abroad instead, which is a real net cost to the country as a whole.
Government borrowing to finance the deficit adds to the demand for loanable funds, which can push up the real interest rate. A higher real interest rate makes fewer private investment projects profitable (recall the investment demand curve from Chapter 10), so some private investment gets “crowded out” by government borrowing.

title: Chapter 14: Money, the Federal Reserve, and Interest Rates
text:
Problem 1: Money Market Equilibrium
An economy’s nominal GDP is $1,800 billion, and transactions demand for money equals \(0.20 \times\) nominal GDP. Asset demand for money follows the schedule \(600 - 40r\) (in billions), where \(r\) is the interest rate in percent. The money supply is fixed at $840 billion.

What is transactions demand for money?
Write total money demand as a function of the interest rate \(r\).
Find the equilibrium interest rate.
Nominal GDP rises to $2,400 billion. Find the new transactions demand and the new equilibrium interest rate. Does the equilibrium quantity of money change? Why or why not?



Show Answer



                            
                                            



Transactions demand \(= 0.20 \times 1{,}800 = \$360\) billion.
Total money demand \(= 360 + (600 - 40r) = 960 - 40r\).
Set demand equal to supply: \(960 - 40r = 840 \Rightarrow 40r = 120 \Rightarrow r = 3\) percent.
New transactions demand \(= 0.20 \times 2{,}400 = \$480\) billion. New equilibrium: \(1{,}080 - 40r = 840 \Rightarrow r = 6\) percent. The equilibrium quantity of money does not change, it stays at $840 billion, because the money supply curve is vertical (fixed by the Fed), so the entire adjustment to higher money demand happens through a higher interest rate, not a larger quantity of money.

title: Chapter 14: Money, the Federal Reserve, and Interest Rates
text:
Problem 2: Bond Prices and Yields
A particular bond has no fixed maturity date and pays a fixed $600 per year forever (a perpetuity).

If the bond currently sells for $6,000, what yield (interest rate) does it offer a buyer?
If the bond’s price rises to $7,500, what is the new yield?
If the bond’s price rises further to $10,000, what is the yield?
As the bond’s price rose from $6,000 to $10,000, what happened to its yield? Explain briefly why this makes sense using the relationship between a bond’s fixed payment and its price.



Show Answer



                            
                                            



Yield \(= 600/6{,}000 = 0.10 = 10\) percent.
Yield \(= 600/7{,}500 = 0.08 = 8\) percent.
Yield \(= 600/10{,}000 = 0.06 = 6\) percent.
The yield fell from 10 percent to 6 percent as the price rose. Because the bond’s future payment is fixed at $600 regardless of price, paying more today for that same fixed payment means earning a smaller return on your money, which is exactly why bond prices and interest rates move inversely.

section: Problem 3: How New Loans Expand the Money Supply
text:
Problem 3: How New Loans Expand the Money Supply
A local bank currently holds $500,000 in checkable deposits. A business takes out a new $80,000 loan from the bank, and the bank deposits the loan amount directly into the business’s checking account at that same bank.

Immediately after the loan is made, what happens to total checkable deposits at the bank?
Explain, in your own words, why making a loan creates new money rather than simply moving existing money from one place to another.
Suppose instead that borrowers across the economy pay down $50,000 more in existing loans than new loans are issued this month. What happens to checkable deposits, and therefore the money supply, as a result?



Show Answer


Checkable deposits rise from $500,000 to $580,000 ($500,000 \(+\) $80,000).
The loan does not come out of an existing depositor’s account, it is genuinely new purchasing power created by the bank, backed by the borrower’s promise to repay. The business now has an extra $80,000 in its checking account that did not exist as spendable money before the loan was made, this is how the banking system expands the money supply beyond the paper currency originally deposited.
Checkable deposits, and the money supply, shrink by the net $50,000, since more loans were retired than newly created. This is the same expansion process running in reverse.

title: Chapter 1: Limits, Alternatives, and Choices
section: Problem 2: Opportunity Cost with Two Goods
text:
Problem 2: Opportunity Cost with Two Goods
A society produces two goods, pizzas and pizza ovens. It is currently producing at point C: 45 units of pizzas and 11 units of pizza ovens. Two other attainable points on the same production possibilities curve are point B (60 pizzas, 6 ovens) and point D (30 pizzas, 15 ovens).

Using points B and C, what is the opportunity cost of one more unit of pizzas?
Using points C and D, what is the opportunity cost of one more unit of pizza ovens?



Show Answer


Moving from C to B: pizzas rise by 15 (60 minus 45), ovens fall by 5 (11 minus 6). Giving up ovens to get pizzas: 5 ovens divided by 15 pizzas equals 0.33 ovens per pizza. The opportunity cost of one more pizza is about a third of an oven.
Moving from C to D: pizzas fall by 15 (45 minus 30), ovens rise by 4 (15 minus 11). Giving up pizzas to get ovens: 15 pizzas divided by 4 ovens equals 3.75 pizzas per oven. The opportunity cost of one more pizza oven is 3.75 pizzas.

Notice the two answers are not simple reciprocals of each other, since the curve is not a straight line, the opportunity cost changes depending on which section of the curve you are on. That is the law of increasing opportunity cost in action.

Transfer payments ($80): no good or service is produced in exchange. Purchases of existing stocks and bonds ($45): just a transfer of ownership of existing financial assets, not production. Sales of secondhand goods ($12): those goods were counted in GDP when they were first produced.

Calculate national income (NI) by adding up the types of income and taxes on production and imports.
Calculate GDP and NDP using the income approach.
Calculate personal income (PI).
Calculate disposable income (DI).
What share of national income is compensation of employees?



Show Answer



                            
                                            



NI \(= 560 + 20 + 30 + 70 + 110 + 65 = \$855\) billion.
GDP \(=\) NI \(+\) depreciation \(= 855 + 90 = \$945\) billion. NDP \(=\) GDP \(-\) depreciation \(= \$855\) billion (equal to NI here because the statistical discrepancy and net foreign factor income are zero).

Transfer payments reach households without being earned by producing anything, so they are added.

section: Problem 3: Nominal vs. Real GDP with Multiple Goods
text:
Problem 3: Nominal vs. Real GDP with Multiple Goods
A small economy produces only two goods, coffee and phone chargers. Prices and quantities in Year 1 (the base year) and Year 2 are:




Year 1 Price
Year 1 Quantity
Year 2 Price
Year 2 Quantity




Coffee
$2
100
$3
120


Phone chargers
$5
40
$6
45




Compute nominal GDP in Year 1 and in Year 2.
Compute real GDP in Year 2, using Year 1 as the base year (that is, value Year 2 quantities at Year 1 prices).
What is the nominal GDP growth rate from Year 1 to Year 2? What is the real GDP growth rate?
These two growth rates are quite different. What does that difference tell you about what actually happened in this economy?



Show Answer


Nominal GDP, Year 1: \((2 \times 100) + (5 \times 40) = 200 + 200 = \$400\). Nominal GDP, Year 2: \((3 \times 120) + (6 \times 45) = 360 + 270 = \$630\).
Real GDP, Year 2 (in Year 1 prices): \((2 \times 120) + (5 \times 45) = 240 + 225 = \$465\).
Nominal GDP growth: \((630 - 400)/400 = 57.5\) percent. Real GDP growth: \((465 - 400)/400 = 16.25\) percent.
Nominal GDP growth (57.5 percent) reflects both more output and higher prices for both goods. Real GDP growth (16.25 percent) strips out the price increases by valuing both years’ output at the same, Year 1, prices, so it isolates how much more stuff the economy actually produced. The large gap between the two growth rates tells us that a substantial part of this economy’s nominal growth was simply inflation, not a real increase in output, which is exactly why economists track real GDP rather than nominal GDP when asking whether an economy is actually producing more.

By how much did the overall price level rise from 2022 to 2024? How does that compare with the gap between the two growth rates in part (b)?



Show Answer



                            
                                            



Real GDP \(=\) nominal GDP \(/ (\text{index}/100)\). 2020: \(1{,}800 / 1.00 = \$1{,}800\) billion. 2022: \(2{,}160 / 1.08 = \$2{,}000\) billion. 2024: \(2{,}600 / 1.25 = \$2{,}080\) billion.

Problem 5: Is Higher GDP Per Capita Always Better?
Two countries have these (hypothetical) figures per person per year:









Country A
Country B




Measured GDP per capita
$50,000
$46,000

Which country has the higher measured GDP per capita?

Despite these shortcomings, why do economists still rely on GDP so heavily?



Show Answer


Country A: $50,000 versus $46,000 for Country B.
Country A: $50,000 \(+\) $8,000 \(=\) $58,000. Country B: $46,000 \(+\) $14,000 \(=\) $60,000. Once unpaid work is counted, Country B comes out ahead, the ranking flips.
Leisure: Country B residents work ten fewer hours each week and get twice as much vacation, and GDP assigns that free time no value at all. GDP is measured consistently across countries and over time, follows clear rules, and is strongly correlated with many things people care about, like life expectancy and education. It is an imperfect but useful measure of a country’s production, not a complete measure of its well-being.

In a small town, 142 people are employed and 8 are actively looking for work but do not have a job. What is the size of the labor force?

section: Problem 1: The Labor Force and the Unemployment Rate
text:
Problem 1: The Labor Force and the Unemployment Rate
A regional economy has a working-age population of 500,000 people. Of these, 60,000 are retired, full-time students, or otherwise not looking for work. Of the people who remain, 405,000 currently have jobs.

How many people are in the labor force?
How many people are unemployed?
What is the unemployment rate?
What is the labor force participation rate (labor force divided by the working-age population)?
Suppose 5,000 unemployed workers become discouraged and stop looking for work altogether, with no other changes. What happens to the labor force, the unemployment rate, and the labor force participation rate?



Show Answer


Labor force \(= 500{,}000 - 60{,}000 = 440{,}000\).
Unemployed \(= 440{,}000 - 405{,}000 = 35{,}000\).
Unemployment rate \(= 35{,}000 / 440{,}000 \approx 8.0\) percent.
Participation rate \(= 440{,}000 / 500{,}000 = 88.0\) percent.
The labor force shrinks to \(435{,}000\) (those 5,000 people are no longer counted as looking for work). Unemployed falls to \(30{,}000\), so the unemployment rate becomes \(30{,}000/435{,}000 \approx 6.9\) percent, it falls, even though nobody found a job. The participation rate falls to \(435{,}000/500{,}000 = 87.0\) percent. This is a classic case where a falling unemployment rate does not necessarily mean the job market improved.

title: Chapter 9: Business Cycles, Unemployment, and Inflation
section: Problem 3: Who Wins and Who Loses from Inflation?
text:
Problem 3: Who Wins and Who Loses from Inflation?
Inflation over one year turns out to be 6 percent, higher than almost anyone expected.

A retiree lives on a pension fixed at $2,400 per month in nominal dollars. What happens to the real value of that pension over the year?
A homeowner has a 30-year mortgage with a fixed interest rate of 4 percent, borrowed before the inflation surprise. Are they better off or worse off because of the unexpectedly high inflation? Why?
A worker’s employer raises her nominal salary from $58,000 to $60,500 for the year. Is her real income rising or falling? By approximately how much?
Based on (a) through (c), state in one sentence who tends to gain and who tends to lose from unanticipated inflation.



Show Answer


The pension stays fixed in nominal dollars, but prices rose 6 percent, so its real purchasing power falls by roughly 6 percent.
Better off. They are repaying a fixed 4 percent rate with dollars that are now worth less than expected, unanticipated inflation transfers real value from lenders to borrowers with fixed-rate debt.
Nominal salary grew \((60{,}500-58{,}000)/58{,}000 \approx 4.3\) percent, which is less than the 6 percent inflation rate, so her real income falls by roughly \(4.3 - 6 = -1.7\) percent.
Losers tend to be people with fixed nominal incomes and savers or lenders holding fixed-rate debt; winners tend to be borrowers repaying fixed-rate debt with money that is now worth less.

title: Chapter 9: Business Cycles, Unemployment, and Inflation
section: Problem 4: Business Cycle Phases and the Cost of Inflation
text:
Problem 4: Business Cycle Phases and the Cost of Inflation

Put these four phases of the business cycle in order, starting from a business cycle peak: trough, expansion, peak, recession.
During a recession, which industry would you expect to see a larger drop in sales: a grocery store, or a company that manufactures new cars? Explain using the idea of postponable spending.
A country’s inflation rate accelerates from a modest 3 percent to over 200 percent per year (hyperinflation). Name two ways this could damage the economy’s total output, beyond simply making goods more expensive.
Explain briefly why even a low, stable, fully anticipated inflation rate (say, 2 percent) still imposes some real cost on an economy, rather than being completely harmless.



Show Answer


Peak, recession, trough, expansion, and then back toward a new peak.
The car manufacturer. Cars are a durable good, and durable-good purchases can be postponed, a household can keep driving its current car for another year or two if money is tight. Grocery spending on food is much harder to postpone, so it holds up better in a downturn.
Any two reasonable answers, for example: people rush to spend money immediately before it loses more value, which disrupts normal saving and planning; businesses struggle to set prices and sign contracts when prices change by the day or hour; normal exchange breaks down as money stops functioning as a reliable store of value, all of which can cause total output to fall sharply.
Even fully anticipated inflation imposes menu costs (the real resources businesses spend updating posted prices, menus, and contracts) and shoe-leather costs (the time and effort people spend trying to avoid holding cash that is losing value, such as more frequent trips to the bank). These are real resources used up simply coping with inflation rather than producing goods and services.

text:
Problem 1: Small Growth Differences, Compounded
Country A and Country B both start with real GDP per capita of $8,000. Country A grows at 2 percent per year. Country B grows at 4 percent per year.

Using the Rule of 70, how many years does it take each country to double its GDP per capita?
Estimate each country’s real GDP per capita after 35 years by compounding the growth rate year by year.
How many times larger is Country B’s GDP per capita than Country A’s after 35 years?
Both countries started at the same GDP per capita and neither growth rate sounds dramatic in a single year. What does this problem illustrate about long-run growth?



Show Answer



                            
                                            



Country A: \(70/2 = 35\) years. Country B: \(70/4 = 17.5\) years.
Country A: \(8{,}000 \times 1.02^{35} \approx \$16{,}000\). Country B: \(8{,}000 \times 1.04^{35} \approx \$31{,}600\).
\(31{,}600 / 16{,}000 \approx 2.0\), Country B’s GDP per capita is about twice Country A’s after 35 years, even though B’s doubling time is only half of A’s.
A growth rate that looks small year to year, a gap of just 2 percentage points here, compounds into an enormous difference in living standards over a working lifetime. This is exactly why economists care so much about small, sustained differences in growth rates rather than dismissing them as trivial.

title: Chapter 8: Economic Growth
section: Problem 2: Where Does Growth Come From?
text:
Problem 2: Where Does Growth Come From?
An economy’s real GDP grew by approximately 3.2 percent over one year. Economists estimate that total hours worked in the economy grew by 0.9 percent over the same year.

Approximately what was the growth rate of labor productivity (output per hour) that year?
If, instead, hours worked had fallen by 0.4 percent while real GDP still grew 3.2 percent, approximately what would labor productivity growth have been?
In part (b), the economy produced more total output with fewer hours worked. What does that imply about labor productivity, and why might that be a healthier long-run growth pattern than growth driven mainly by more hours worked?



Show Answer


Real GDP growth is approximately labor input growth plus productivity growth, so \(3.2 - 0.9 = 2.3\) percent productivity growth.
\(3.2 - (-0.4) = 3.6\) percent productivity growth.
It implies productivity grew faster than total output, each hour worked produced substantially more. Growth driven by rising productivity can continue indefinitely as workers and firms find better technology, tools, and methods, while growth driven mainly by working more hours runs into a hard limit, there are only so many hours in a day and so many working-age people. Sustained increases in living standards ultimately depend on productivity growth, not on people simply working more.

title: Chapter 8: Economic Growth
section: Problem 3: Is Faster Growth Always Better?
text:
Problem 3: Is Faster Growth Always Better?
A country is debating a policy that would raise its long-run real GDP growth rate from 2.0 percent to 3.0 percent per year, mainly by encouraging more saving, investment in new capital, and faster adoption of new technology.

Using the Rule of 70, how much sooner would the country’s GDP per capita double under the faster growth rate?
Name one real resource cost this faster growth might require today, connecting back to the Chapter 6 saving and investment tradeoff.
Suppose the policy succeeds in raising average GDP per capita, but nearly all of the additional growth goes to the top of the income distribution. Connecting back to Chapter 6, why might the typical household not feel much better off, even though the national statistics look better?
Name one non-income cost that faster growth might impose that GDP per capita does not capture at all.



Show Answer


Doubling time at 2 percent: \(70/2 = 35\) years. At 3 percent: \(70/3 \approx 23.3\) years. The faster growth rate would cut the doubling time by roughly 12 years.
More investment in new capital means less current consumption, resources devoted to building factories, machines, and infrastructure today are resources not used to produce consumer goods today. That is the same saving-versus-consumption tradeoff from Chapter 6.
GDP per capita is a mean. If growth is concentrated among a small share of households, the mean can rise substantially while the median household’s income barely changes, the same mean-versus-median gap discussed in Chapter 6.
Any reasonable answer describing an externality or nonmarket cost is acceptable, for example: environmental damage from more production, resource depletion, or less leisure time if the faster growth comes from working more rather than working smarter.

If the MPS rises, does the simple spending multiplier (\(1/MPS\)) get larger or smaller?

text:
Problem 2: The Multiplier in Action
A new employer moves to town and immediately spends $80 million building a facility. Suppose the MPC in this local economy is 0.6.

What is the MPS?
What is the simple spending multiplier?
What is the total eventual change in local income from this initial $80 million in spending?
Show the first four rounds of the spending chain (the initial spending, then each subsequent round of re-spending).
If local residents instead had an MPC of only 0.4, would the total impact on local income be larger or smaller than in part (c)? Explain in one sentence.



Show Answer



                            
                                            



\(MPS = 1 - 0.6 = 0.4\).
Multiplier \(= 1/MPS = 1/0.4 = 2.5\).
Total change in income \(= \$80\text{M} \times 2.5 = \$200\) million.
Round 1: \(80.00\) million (the initial spending). Round 2: \(80 \times 0.6 = \$48.00\) million. Round 3: \(48.00 \times 0.6 = \$28.80\) million. Round 4: \(28.80 \times 0.6 \approx \$17.28\) million. Each round is smaller than the last, since some of each round’s income leaks into saving rather than being re-spent.

title: Chapter 17: Extending the Analysis of Aggregate Supply
text:
If real GDP is temporarily above potential GDP, what eventually happens to nominal wages, and which direction does SRAS shift as a result?
If real GDP is temporarily below potential GDP, what eventually happens to nominal wages (even though this happens slowly), and which direction does SRAS shift as a result?
On the short-run Phillips curve, is the relationship between unemployment and inflation positive or negative?
Is the long-run Phillips curve upward sloping, downward sloping, or vertical? At what unemployment rate does it sit?
If unemployment is temporarily below the natural rate and inflation is rising, is this a short-run or a long-run Phillips curve situation?
Why does the short-run unemployment-inflation tradeoff eventually disappear as expected inflation catches up to actual inflation?



Show Answer


Nominal wages eventually rise (firms compete for workers in a tight labor market), which shifts SRAS left.
Nominal wages eventually fall, though slowly since wages are sticky downward, which shifts SRAS right.
Negative (inverse): lower unemployment tends to come with higher inflation, and vice versa.
Vertical, at the natural rate of unemployment.
Short-run. The long run is defined by the economy having fully adjusted back to the natural rate of unemployment, regardless of the inflation rate.
Once expected inflation rises to match actual inflation, the short-run Phillips curve itself shifts, and the temporary tradeoff vanishes, unemployment drifts back toward the natural rate even if inflation remains elevated.

title: Chapter 17: Extending the Analysis of Aggregate Supply
section: Problem 1: Self-Correction After an Inflationary Gap
text:
Problem 1: Self-Correction After an Inflationary Gap
An economy’s potential GDP is 400 (illustrative units). AD is fixed at \(AD(P) = 600 - 4(P-90)\). The original short-run supply curve is \(SRAS_0(P) = 400 + 4(P-90)\).

Find the short-run equilibrium price level and real GDP where \(AD(P) = SRAS_0(P)\).
Is this equilibrium’s real GDP above, below, or equal to potential GDP? What is this gap called?
Over time, self-correction shifts the supply curve to \(SRAS_1(P) = 200 + 4(P-90)\). Find the new equilibrium where \(AD(P) = SRAS_1(P)\).
Compare the new equilibrium’s real GDP to potential GDP. What happened to the price level between the two equilibria?



Show Answer



                            
                                            



Setting \(600-4(P-90)=400+4(P-90)\): \(200=8(P-90) \Rightarrow P-90=25 \Rightarrow P=115\). Real GDP \(= 400+4(25)=500\).
Real GDP (500) is above potential GDP (400). This is an inflationary gap.
Setting \(600-4(P-90)=200+4(P-90)\): \(400=8(P-90) \Rightarrow P-90=50 \Rightarrow P=140\). Real GDP \(=200+4(50)=400\).
The new equilibrium’s real GDP (400) now exactly equals potential GDP, the economy has fully self-corrected. The price level rose, from 115 to 140, and settled permanently higher, exactly the pattern predicted: an inflationary gap closes through rising nominal wages, shrinking SRAS, and a higher long-run price level, not through any change in long-run output.

title: Chapter 17: Extending the Analysis of Aggregate Supply
section: Problem 2: Reading the Short-Run Phillips Curve
text:
Problem 2: Reading the Short-Run Phillips Curve
A short-run Phillips curve is given by the relationship: inflation rate \(= 10 - u\), where \(u\) is the unemployment rate (in percent). The natural rate of unemployment in this economy is 5 percent.

What is the inflation rate when unemployment is 4 percent?
What is the inflation rate when unemployment is 8 percent?
What is the inflation rate when unemployment is exactly at the natural rate (5 percent)?
Explain why this same short-run Phillips curve is really just another way of drawing the demand-pull side of the AD/AS model from Chapter 12.



Show Answer



                            
                                            



Inflation \(= 10 - 4 = 6\) percent.
Inflation \(= 10 - 8 = 2\) percent.
Inflation \(= 10 - 5 = 5\) percent.
Higher AD (demand-pull inflation) both raises the price level and raises real GDP, which means more hiring and lower unemployment. The same underlying demand-pull story that raises the price level and real GDP together in the AD/AS model also raises inflation while lowering unemployment, just plotted on different axes.

title: Chapter 17: Extending the Analysis of Aggregate Supply
text:
Problem 3: When Expected Inflation Rises
A short-run Phillips curve is \(\pi = \pi^e - (u - 5)\), where \(\pi\) is actual inflation, \(u\) is the unemployment rate (in percent), \(\pi^e\) is expected inflation, and 5 percent is the natural rate of unemployment.

If expected inflation \(\pi^e = 3\) percent, what is actual inflation when unemployment is exactly at the natural rate (5 percent)?
Still with \(\pi^e = 3\) percent, suppose the economy overheats and unemployment falls to 3 percent. What is actual inflation now?
Now suppose expected inflation has risen to \(\pi^e = 6\) percent (people have come to expect more inflation, based on recent experience), with unemployment still at 3 percent. What is actual inflation?
Compare your answers to (b) and (c). What happened to the short-run Phillips curve itself as expected inflation rose? At the natural rate of unemployment, does actual inflation ever differ from expected inflation in this model?



Show Answer


\(\pi = 3 - (5-5) = 3 - 0 = 3\) percent. At the natural rate, the \((u-5)\) term is zero, so actual inflation simply equals expected inflation.
\(\pi = 3 - (3-5) = 3 + 2 = 5\) percent. With unemployment below the natural rate, actual inflation runs above expected inflation, the short-run tradeoff at work.
\(\pi = 6 - (3-5) = 6 + 2 = 8\) percent.
Comparing (b) and (c), at the same unemployment rate (3 percent), actual inflation rose from 5 to 8 percent, exactly the 3 percentage point rise in expected inflation. The entire short-run Phillips curve shifted up by that amount. And at the natural rate of unemployment specifically, actual inflation always exactly equals expected inflation, whatever that happens to be, there is no stable, exploitable tradeoff there: unemployment cannot be held permanently below the natural rate just by tolerating ever-higher inflation, once expectations catch up, only inflation ends up permanently higher, not unemployment permanently lower.

title: Chapter 16: Financial Economics
text:
A city issues bonds to pay for a new bridge. Is this an economic investment, a financial investment, or both?
A retiree buys 100 shares of an existing company’s stock on the stock market. Is this an economic investment, a financial investment, or both?
Money available today is generally worth more than the same dollar amount available a year from now. Why?
What is diversifiable (idiosyncratic) risk? Can it be reduced by holding many different stocks?
What is nondiversifiable (systemic) risk? Can it be reduced by diversifying?
Why do corporate bonds typically pay a higher interest rate than government bonds of similar maturity?



Show Answer


Economic investment. The bond issuance finances new capital, an addition to society’s capital stock (a new bridge).
Financial investment only. The retiree is exchanging money for an existing asset, ownership simply transfers from the seller to the retiree, no new capital is created.
Because money available today can be invested to earn interest, growing into a larger amount by the time that future date arrives.
Diversifiable risk is risk specific to one company or asset (a product recall, a lawsuit, a bad quarter). Yes, it can be reduced or eliminated by holding many different assets, since bad luck at one company is unlikely to hit all your other holdings at the same time.
Nondiversifiable risk affects the whole market or economy (a recession, a broad market crash). No, holding more assets does not protect you from a risk that affects nearly everything at once.
Because corporate bonds carry more default risk than government bonds, investors demand a higher rate of return to compensate for the greater chance the corporation cannot repay.

text:
Problem 1: Present Value

You are promised $1,210 exactly one year from now. If the interest rate is 10 percent, what is the present value of that payment today?
You are instead promised $1,210 exactly two years from now, still at a 10 percent interest rate. What is its present value today?
Why is your answer to (b) smaller than your answer to (a), even though both promise the exact same future dollar amount?



Show Answer



                            
                                            



\(X_0 = X_t/(1+i)^t = 1{,}210/(1.10)^1 = \$1{,}100\).
\(X_0 = 1{,}210/(1.10)^2 = 1{,}210/1.21 = \$1{,}000\).
Waiting longer for the same future payment means giving up more potential interest earnings along the way, so a payment further in the future is worth less today than the same payment arriving sooner.

title: Chapter 16: Financial Economics
text:
Problem 2: Comparing Two Payment Streams
The interest rate is 8 percent. Compare two hypothetical assets:

Asset A pays a single lump sum of $1,080, exactly one year from now.
Asset B pays $540 one year from now, and $583.20 two years from now.


Compute the present value of Asset A.
Compute the present value of each of Asset B’s two payments, and their sum.
Should Asset A and Asset B trade at the same price today? Why or why not?



Show Answer


\(PV_A = 1{,}080/1.08 = \$1{,}000\).
First payment: \(540/1.08 = \$500\). Second payment: \(583.20/(1.08)^2 = 583.20/1.1664 = \$500\). Sum: \(500 + 500 = \$1{,}000\).
Yes. Both assets have the exact same present value, $1,000, even though they pay out different amounts on different schedules. Since investors care about present value, not the raw sum of future dollars, the two assets should be priced identically today.

Problem 3: Stock Returns and Bond Risk

A share of stock in Meridian Corp costs $60 and pays an annual dividend of $3. What is its (dividend-only) rate of return?
A similar company, Alderbrook Inc., pays the same $3 dividend but its stock costs only $50. What is Alderbrook’s rate of return? If both stocks are otherwise equally risky, what would you expect investors to do, and what effect would that have on Alderbrook’s stock price?
Rank the following bonds from lowest to highest expected interest rate, and briefly explain your reasoning: (i) a 2-year U.S. government bond, (ii) a 10-year U.S. government bond, (iii) a 10-year corporate bond from a financially shaky company.



Show Answer


Rate of return \(= 3/60 = 5\) percent.
Rate of return \(= 3/50 = 6\) percent. Since Alderbrook offers a higher return for similar risk, investors would sell Meridian stock to buy Alderbrook stock. That buying pressure would push Alderbrook’s price up (and Meridian’s price down), narrowing the gap in returns between the two, similar assets tend toward similar returns.
Lowest to highest: (i) the 2-year U.S. government bond (lowest risk, shortest wait), then (ii) the 10-year U.S. government bond (same low default risk, but investors demand more for tying up money longer), then (iii) the 10-year corporate bond from a shaky company (highest, both long maturity and meaningful default risk).

title: Chapter 11: The Aggregate Expenditures Model
text:
In the aggregate expenditures model, prices are assumed to be sticky in the short run. When total spending changes, does that show up mainly as a change in real output or a change in prices?
True or False: equilibrium GDP always equals potential (full-employment) GDP.
At a GDP level where planned spending (AE) is greater than actual output, what happens to unplanned inventories, and which direction does that push future production?
At a GDP level where planned spending (AE) is less than actual output, what happens to unplanned inventories, and which direction does that push future production?
If the MPC in an economy is 0.75, what is the simple multiplier?
A country’s aggregate expenditures at full-employment GDP fall $15 billion short of what is needed to reach full-employment GDP. Is this a recessionary or an inflationary expenditure gap?



Show Answer


Real output. Because prices are sticky in the short run, changes in spending are absorbed by changes in how much firms produce, not by changing prices.
False. Equilibrium GDP is simply where planned spending equals output, it can sit above, below, or exactly at potential GDP.
Unplanned inventories fall (firms sell more than they planned to produce), signaling firms to increase production, pushing GDP up toward equilibrium.
Unplanned inventories rise (firms sell less than they planned to produce), signaling firms to decrease production, pushing GDP down toward equilibrium.
\(1/(1-0.75) = 1/0.25 = 4\).
A recessionary expenditure gap (spending falls short at full employment, producing a negative GDP gap).

section: Problem 2: Adding Government Spending and Taxes
text:
Problem 2: Adding Government Spending and Taxes
Starting from the private economy in Problem 1 (equilibrium GDP \(= \$800\) billion, MPC \(=0.75\)), the government now adds \(G = \$50\) billion in purchases.

By how much does the AE schedule shift at every GDP level?
Using the multiplier from Problem 1(d), by how much does equilibrium GDP change? What is the new equilibrium GDP?
The government now also imposes a lump-sum tax of \(T = \$100\) billion. Since \(MPC=0.75\), consumption falls by \(MPC \times T = 0.75 \times 100 = \$75\) billion at every GDP level. Using the multiplier, what is the tax’s effect on equilibrium GDP by itself?
Combining the effects of \(G\) and \(T\) from parts (b) and (c), what is the new equilibrium GDP?



Show Answer


AE shifts up by the full $50 billion at every GDP level (government purchases add directly to spending).
\(\Delta GDP = \text{multiplier} \times \Delta G = 4 \times 50 = \$200\) billion. New equilibrium GDP (with G only) \(= 800 + 200 = \$1{,}000\) billion.
The tax reduces AE by \(MPC \times T = \$75\) billion at every GDP level. Its effect on equilibrium GDP alone: \(-4 \times 75 = -\$300\) billion.
Combining both effects from the original \(\$800\) billion baseline: \(800 + 200 - 300 = \$700\) billion. Show Answer



                            
                                            



\(\Delta GDP = 4 \times 50 = \$200\) billion. New equilibrium GDP \(= 700 + 200 = \$900\) billion.

At \(GDP=1{,}100\), \(AE=1{,}050\), which is \(\$50\) billion short of the \(1{,}100\) needed. The recessionary expenditure gap is $50 billion.
To close a \(\$50\) billion AE shortfall using a multiplier of \(4\): it would take a \(\$50\) billion increase in spending to shift the whole AE line up by \(50\), which raises equilibrium GDP by \(4 \times 50 = \$200\) billion, exactly closing the gap from \(900\) to the full-employment level of \(1{,}100\).

text:

Demand shifts left. Both equilibrium price and quantity decrease.

A college places a $50 price ceiling on textbooks to control costs for students. How many textbooks actually get sold at that price?
While the ceiling is in effect, a new printing technology lowers production costs, shifting supply to the right. What happens to the number of textbooks actually sold?



Show Answer



                            
                                            



Equilibrium is $60, where quantity demanded and quantity supplied both equal 1,200.
At the $50 ceiling, quantity demanded is 2,200 but quantity supplied is only 600. The number of textbooks actually sold is capped by the shorter side of the market, so only 600 get sold, even though far more students want one at that price. This leaves a shortage of 1,600 books.
A rightward shift in supply means more textbooks are supplied at every price, including $50. As long as the ceiling is still below the new equilibrium price, more textbooks get sold than before (still capped by supply, but a higher supply quantity), narrowing the shortage. In the graph above, quantity supplied at the $50 ceiling rises from 600 to 900, so the shortage shrinks from 1,600 to 1,300 books.

title: Chapter 3: Supply, Demand, and Market Equilibrium
text:
Problem 3: Concert Tickets and StubHub
A popular artist announces a stadium tour. Tickets go on sale through the venue at a fixed face price of $150, but the stadium only has 50,000 seats.

Draw or describe what happens to the demand curve for this concert compared to a typical touring act, and explain why.
At the $150 face price, is the quantity of tickets demanded larger or smaller than the quantity supplied (50,000 seats)? What does that imply happens in a resale market like StubHub?
Suppose resale tickets end up selling for $600. Using the supply and demand model, explain why the resale price is so much higher than the face price, even though it is the same seats being sold.
Discussion: A small number of platforms (like Live Nation-Ticketmaster) control both primary ticket sales and much of the resale market for major tours, and have faced antitrust scrutiny over this. Does having one dominant platform change how well the basic supply-and-demand model predicts ticket prices? Why or why not?
Airline seats on a specific flight are also fixed in number once the plane is scheduled. Is the short-run supply curve for seats on a given flight similarly vertical? Given that, why do airline tickets not typically show up on a resale market the way concert tickets do?



Show Answer



                            
                                            



Demand for this concert shifts far to the right relative to a typical touring act; at every price, many more people want a ticket, because the artist’s popularity increases how much value fans place on attending.
Supply is fixed at 50,000 seats no matter the price (a vertical supply curve, at least in the short run for a specific show date). If quantity demanded at $150 is far above 50,000, there is an excess quantity demanded at the face price, some people who want a ticket at $150 will not get one, which creates the incentive for a resale market to exist.
Because supply is fixed, the face price of $150 does not do the job of rationing the limited seats to only the people willing to pay the most. The resale price is close to the price at which quantity demanded actually equals quantity supplied (50,000) once the artificially low face price is removed, that market-clearing price reflects how much buyers are truly willing to pay for a scarce good.
Open discussion. The basic model still explains the direction of the price (fixed supply and high demand push price up), but a dominant platform may be able to set or influence prices and fees beyond what a fully competitive resale market would produce, which is a market power question the simple supply-and-demand model does not fully capture. This is a preview of ideas covered when we study market structure later in the course.
Yes, the number of seats on a specific flight is also fixed once the plane is set, so short-run supply for that one flight is vertical too, just like a single concert. The key difference is on the pricing and transfer side, airlines themselves practice extensive dynamic pricing, raising the fare many times as a flight fills up, so the airline (not a third party) captures most of the value that would otherwise go to scalpers. Airline tickets are also typically non-transferable (tied to a passenger’s name and ID), which blocks a resale market from forming the way concert tickets can be resold. One more difference worth noting: a concert is one venue with a fixed number of seats, but “airline seats” as a market means many airlines choosing flight frequency, routes, and plane size. Looking across a whole market like that, and over a longer time frame, supply does start to look like a normal upward-sloping curve rather than a single vertical line, airlines can and do add more seats when prices (and profits) are high. The vertical-supply story applies best to one specific, already-scheduled flight in the very short run.

section: Problem 4: The Used Car Market During a Computer Chip Shortage
text:
Problem 4: The Used Car Market During a Computer Chip Shortage
In 2021, a global shortage of semiconductor chips forced automakers to slow down new car production, since modern cars need chips to run everything from engines to infotainment systems.

What happens to the supply of new cars during the chip shortage? Which direction does the new car supply curve shift?
As new cars become harder to find, many buyers turn to the used car market instead. What happens to the demand curve for used cars, and why?
At the same time, some used car owners decide to hold onto their vehicles longer rather than sell, since replacing the car would be difficult and expensive. What happens to the supply curve for used cars?
Using your answers to (b) and (c), explain what happens to the equilibrium price of used cars. Can you say for certain what happens to the equilibrium quantity of used cars sold? Why or why not?



Show Answer



                            
                                            



The chip shortage raises production costs and limits how many new cars manufacturers can actually build, so the new car supply curve shifts left.
With new cars scarce and often more expensive, used cars become a more attractive substitute, so the demand curve for used cars shifts right, more buyers want used cars at every price.
Owners who would normally sell (perhaps to buy a newer car) hold on instead, so fewer used cars are offered for sale at every price, the supply curve for used cars shifts left.
Both shifts, demand right and supply left, push the equilibrium price of used cars up unambiguously (which is exactly what happened in 2021 and 2022). Equilibrium quantity is ambiguous, the rightward demand shift pushes quantity up while the leftward supply shift pushes quantity down, so without knowing the relative size of each shift, we cannot say from the model alone whether more or fewer used cars actually changed hands. In practice, used car sales volume fell even as prices spiked, telling us the supply shift was the dominant force.

title: Chapter 3: Supply, Demand, and Market Equilibrium
text:
Problem 5: The Ozempic Effect
A new class of prescription drugs (GLP-1 medications like Ozempic and Wegovy) is approved for weight loss, in addition to its original use for diabetes. Demand for these drugs surges rapidly, driven by both word of mouth and social media, while manufacturers struggle to build enough production capacity to keep up.

What happens to the demand curve for these drugs, and why?
In the short run, manufacturing capacity for a complex injectable drug cannot expand quickly. What does that imply about the shape of the short-run supply curve, and what happens to price and quantity as a result?
Patients who need the drug for diabetes (its original approved use) report trouble finding it in stock, even though production levels have not fallen. Using the model, explain how a demand shift alone can create a shortage for existing users, without any change in supply.
Over the following two years, manufacturers invest heavily in new factories and production lines, and competing drug makers enter the market with similar products. What happens to the supply curve over this longer time horizon, and what would you expect to happen to price?



Show Answer



                            
                                            



Demand shifts right, a new, large group of potential buyers (people seeking weight loss, not just diabetes management) enters the market, increasing quantity demanded at every price.
In the short run, supply is close to fixed (nearly vertical), since building new manufacturing capacity takes years. With demand shifting right against a nearly fixed short-run supply, the price rises sharply while quantity increases only modestly.
Even though the amount supplied has not decreased, the large rightward shift in demand means quantity demanded now exceeds quantity supplied at the old price. Because there is effectively a price ceiling in practice (insurance-negotiated prices, or simply a price that does not adjust instantly), this excess demand shows up as a shortage, existing patients cannot get the drug even though nothing about supply changed for them specifically. On the graph, holding the price at its original $100 level after demand shifts to D1 shows quantity supplied stuck near 30 (short-run supply barely moves) while quantity demanded jumps to 56, a shortage of 26 units at that price.
As new factories come online and competitors enter, the supply curve shifts right over time. With demand still elevated but supply now catching up, we would expect the equilibrium price to fall from its earlier peak (and quantity to keep rising), which is the standard pattern for markets adjusting to a large demand shock over the longer run.

Method 3: (4 × $3) + (8 × $2) + (2 × $4) + (1 × $10) = $12 + $16 + $8 + $10 = $46

title: Chapter 2: The Market System and the Circular Flow
text:
Problem 2: Self-Interest and Competition
A small town has exactly one hardware store. A national chain announces it is opening a second hardware store two blocks away next year.

Before the new store arrives, what does the existing store’s self-interest push it to do about prices and service quality, given it has no local competitor?
After the new store opens, how does competition change what self-interest pushes the existing store to do?
Explain, in one or two sentences, why economists say it takes self-interest and competition together to benefit consumers, not self-interest alone.



Show Answer


With no competitor, the existing store’s self-interest still points toward profit, but nothing forces that profit-seeking to benefit customers. It could charge higher prices or offer weaker service and customers would have nowhere else to go locally.
Once a competitor opens nearby, self-interest now requires competing for the same customers. The store has an incentive to lower prices, improve service, or both, or risk losing business to the new entrant.
Self-interest alone only guarantees a business tries to maximize its own gain. Competition is what forces that self-interest to serve customers, since a business that ignores customers loses them to a rival. Remove competition and the same self-interested motive can just as easily lead to worse outcomes for consumers.

title: Chapter 12: Aggregate Demand and Aggregate Supply
text:
For each scenario, name which of the three reasons the AD curve slopes downward is at work:

a higher price level erodes the purchasing power of household savings accounts, so people spend less; (ii) a higher price level makes domestic goods pricier than foreign alternatives, reducing exports; (iii) a higher price level increases the demand for money, pushing up interest rates and discouraging interest-sensitive investment.

Is the short-run aggregate supply curve (SRAS) upward sloping or vertical? What about the long-run aggregate supply curve (LRAS)?
Which curve, SRAS or LRAS, reflects the idea that input prices (especially wages) are sticky and have not yet adjusted?
A new technology raises productivity across the whole economy. Does this shift AS right or left?
A key imported input suddenly becomes much more expensive. Does this shift AS right or left?
True or False: an increase in AD moves the price level and real GDP in the same direction, while a decrease in AS (a leftward shift) also raises the price level but lowers real GDP.



Show Answer



The real-balances effect. (ii) The foreign purchases effect. (iii) The interest-rate effect.

SRAS is upward sloping. LRAS is vertical, at the economy’s potential (full-employment) level of real GDP.
SRAS. Because input prices have not yet adjusted, a higher output price level raises firms’ profit margins and encourages more production in the short run.
Right. Higher productivity lets firms produce more at every price level.
Left. Higher input costs reduce firms’ profit margins, so they produce less at every price level.
True. This is exactly the contrast between demand-pull inflation (AD shifts, price level and GDP move together) and cost-push inflation (AS shifts, price level and GDP move in opposite directions).

title: Chapter 12: Aggregate Demand and Aggregate Supply
section: Problem 1: Sizing an AD Shift with the Multiplier
text:
Problem 1: Sizing an AD Shift with the Multiplier
A country’s MPC is 0.8. A wave of business optimism leads firms to increase planned investment spending by $45 billion at every price level.

What is the multiplier?
By how much does this initial change in investment ultimately shift the AD curve (measured in real GDP at a given price level)?
Name one other component of aggregate demand (besides investment) that could shift AD the same way, and briefly explain why.
If MPC had instead been 0.5, would the same $45 billion increase in investment shift AD by more or less than in part (b)? Explain in one sentence.



Show Answer



                            
                                            



Multiplier \(= 1/(1-0.8) = 1/0.2 = 5\).
\(\Delta AD = 45 \times 5 = \$225\) billion.
Any of: an increase in government purchases, a tax cut (which raises consumption), or a rise in net exports, all of these add to spending at every price level and get multiplied the same way investment does.
Less. With MPC \(=0.5\), the multiplier is only \(1/(1-0.5)=2\), so the same $45 billion initial change would shift AD by only \(45 \times 2 = \$90\) billion, less than half of part (b)’s $225 billion.

title: Chapter 12: Aggregate Demand and Aggregate Supply
text:
Problem 2: Demand-Pull vs. Cost-Push Inflation
For each event below, determine whether it causes demand-pull or cost-push inflation, and predict what happens to real GDP alongside the price level.

Consumer confidence surges and households sharply increase spending at every price level.
A major hurricane disrupts oil refineries, sharply raising energy costs for nearly every firm in the economy.
The government significantly increases spending on infrastructure projects.
A new tax is imposed on a key raw material used throughout manufacturing.



Show Answer



                            
                                            



Demand-pull. Consumer spending directly increases AD, shifting it right, price level rises and real GDP rises together (left panel).
Cost-push. Higher energy costs raise production costs economy-wide, shifting SRAS left, price level rises but real GDP falls (right panel), this combination is stagflation.
Demand-pull. Government purchases directly add to AD.
Cost-push. A tax on a widely used input raises production costs, shifting SRAS left.

title: Chapter 15: Monetary Policy, GDP, and the Price Level
text:
To fight a recession, should the Fed use expansionary or contractionary monetary policy? What happens to interest rates under that policy?
Name the Fed’s key policymaking committee that sets the federal funds rate target.
If the Fed wants to lower interest rates through open market operations, does it buy or sell government bonds? (Recall bond prices and interest rates from Chapter 14.)
What is forward guidance, and how can it affect the economy even before the Fed changes any rate?
When are quantitative easing (QE) and quantitative tightening (QT) typically used, compared to ordinary open market operations?
True or False: monetary policy is equally effective at fighting inflation and at pulling an economy out of a severe recession.
Why does the Fed target roughly 2 percent inflation rather than 0 percent?



Show Answer


Expansionary. Interest rates fall.
The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC).
It buys bonds. Buying bonds bids up bond prices, and since bond prices and interest rates move inversely, this pushes interest rates down.
Forward guidance is the Fed communicating its outlook and future policy intentions. If the Fed is credible, businesses and investors adjust their spending and investment plans immediately based on what the Fed says it intends to do, even before any rate actually changes.
QE and QT are typically used when short-term rates are already very low (near the zero lower bound) and the Fed wants to influence longer-term rates directly, ordinary open market operations mainly target short-term rates.
False. Monetary policy is relatively reliable at slowing an overheating economy, but less reliable at pulling an economy out of a severe recession (cyclical asymmetry and the liquidity trap).
A little inflation lets real wages adjust downward even when nominal wages are sticky and rarely get cut outright, this helps labor markets adjust more smoothly than a 0 percent target would.

section: Problem 1: Movement Along vs. a Shift in Investment Demand
text:
Problem 1: Movement Along vs. a Shift in Investment Demand
For each event, determine whether it causes a movement along the investment demand curve or a shift of the entire curve, and explain why.

The Fed actually cuts the federal funds rate target by half a percentage point this week.
The Fed chair gives a speech strongly signaling that rate cuts are likely in the coming months, with no rate change happening yet.
A new technology lowers the cost of building factories across the economy.
Long-term interest rates fall because the Fed begins a new round of quantitative easing.



Show Answer


Movement along the curve. An actual change in the interest rate moves firms along their existing investment demand curve to a new quantity of investment.
Shift of the entire curve (to the right, more investment demanded at every interest rate). No rate has actually changed yet, businesses are adjusting their plans purely because of the credible signal about the future.
Shift of the entire curve (to the right). Lower costs make more projects profitable at every interest rate, this is a change in a non-interest determinant of investment.
Movement along the curve. Even though QE is an unusual tool, it works by actually changing the interest rate (here, a longer-term rate), so it still produces a movement along the existing investment demand curve, not a shift of it.

title: Chapter 15: Monetary Policy, GDP, and the Price Level
section: Problem 2: Tracing the Monetary Policy Transmission Chain
text:
Problem 2: Tracing the Monetary Policy Transmission Chain
The Fed cuts its target interest rate. As a result, businesses find an additional $30 billion in investment projects newly profitable at the lower rate. The economy’s MPC is 0.75.

What chapter’s tool explains why a lower interest rate increases the quantity of investment demanded?
What is the multiplier?
Using the multiplier, by how much does this initial $30 billion increase in investment ultimately shift AD (in real GDP terms)?
In the AD-AS model, what happens to the equilibrium price level and equilibrium real GDP as a result of this AD shift, assuming the economy is not already at potential GDP?



Show Answer



                            
                                            



The investment demand curve (Chapter 10): a lower real interest rate makes more investment projects profitable, increasing the quantity of investment demanded.
Multiplier \(= 1/(1-0.75) = 4\).
\(\Delta AD = 30 \times 4 = \$120\) billion.
Since AD shifts right along the upward-sloping SRAS curve (Chapter 12), the equilibrium price level rises and equilibrium real GDP rises, this is exactly the chain: Fed action to Chapter 10’s investment demand to Chapter 10/11’s multiplier to Chapter 12’s AD-AS equilibrium.

title: Chapter 15: Monetary Policy, GDP, and the Price Level
section: Problem 3: Cyclical Asymmetry and the Liquidity Trap
text:
Problem 3: Cyclical Asymmetry and the Liquidity Trap

During a period of strong demand-pull inflation, the Fed raises interest rates sharply, and borrowing and spending slow noticeably within a few months. Does this illustrate the Fed’s tools working reliably or unreliably?
During a severe recession, the Fed cuts its target rate all the way to nearly zero, but businesses remain too uncertain about the future to borrow, and banks remain too cautious to lend freely. What is this situation called?
In the situation from part (b), what other policy tool (from a previous chapter) might policymakers need to rely on instead?
Explain in one or two sentences why lower interest rates might fail to stimulate borrowing and lending during a severe downturn, even though the same tool works well to cool an overheating economy.



Show Answer


Reliably. This illustrates the “slowing an expansion” side of cyclical asymmetry, where monetary policy tends to work well.
A liquidity trap.
Fiscal policy (Chapter 13), using government spending and taxes to directly boost aggregate demand when monetary policy alone cannot.
Lower rates only stimulate borrowing and lending if businesses are confident enough to invest and banks are confident enough to lend. During a severe downturn, uncertainty about the future can make both sides unwilling to act even at very low rates, breaking the normal chain from lower rates to more investment spending.

text:
A town’s population grows from 8,000 to 8,400 in one year. What is the population growth rate?
A country’s real GDP is $50 million and its population is 25,000. What is real GDP per capita?
A household saves $500 per month. How much total saving does that household contribute in one year?
A $10,000 investment is expected to generate $800 per year in profit. What is the expected rate of return?
A retiree buys 10 shares of an existing company’s stock on the stock market. Does this count as Investment in the economic sense? Why or why not?
A bakery purchases a new industrial oven to expand production. Does this count as Investment in the economic sense? Why or why not?
A landlord signs a 12-month apartment lease with tenants at a fixed monthly rent. Is this price sticky or flexible?
The price of Bitcoin on a cryptocurrency exchange. Is this price sticky or flexible?



Show Answer


\((8{,}400 - 8{,}000)/8{,}000 = 5\) percent.
\(\$50{,}000{,}000 / 25{,}000 = \$2{,}000\) per person.
\(\$500 \times 12 = \$6{,}000\) per year.
\(\$800 / \$10{,}000 = 8\) percent.
No. Buying existing shares just transfers ownership of an already-existing asset from one person to another, it does not create any new capital.
Yes. A new oven is new capital equipment that expands the firm’s ability to produce, exactly what economic Investment means.
Sticky. The rent is locked in by a 12-month lease regardless of changing market conditions.
Flexible. Cryptocurrency prices trade continuously on an exchange and adjust to new information almost instantly.

title: Chapter 6: An Introduction to Macroeconomics
section: Problem 1: Total Growth vs. Per-Capita Growth
text:
Problem 1: Total Growth vs. Per-Capita Growth
A country’s real GDP grows from $18.0 trillion to $18.9 trillion over one year. Over that same year, the country’s population grows from 300 million to 306 million people.

What is the percentage growth rate of total real GDP?
What is real GDP per capita in each year?
What is the percentage growth rate of real GDP per capita?
Why is the answer to (c) smaller than the answer to (a)?



Show Answer


Growth rate of total real GDP = ($18.9 trillion minus $18.0 trillion) divided by $18.0 trillion = $0.9 trillion divided by $18.0 trillion = 5.0 percent.
Real GDP per capita, year 1: $18.0 trillion divided by 300 million = $60,000. Year 2: $18.9 trillion divided by 306 million = $61,765 (rounded).
Growth rate of real GDP per capita = ($61,765 minus $60,000) divided by $60,000 = about 2.9 percent.
Total output grew 5.0 percent, but population also grew (from 300 million to 306 million, a 2.0 percent increase). Since that larger output has to be divided among more people, the increase in living standards per person is smaller than the increase in total output. This is why economists track GDP per capita, not just total GDP, when asking whether people are actually getting better off.

title: Chapter 6: An Introduction to Macroeconomics
section: Problem 2: Saving, Investment, and Expected Returns
text:
Problem 2: Saving, Investment, and Expected Returns
A firm is deciding whether to build a new factory that costs $5 million. The firm forecasts the factory would generate $600,000 in additional profit per year.

What annual rate of return does the firm expect on this $5 million investment?
If interest rates rise and the firm could instead earn a guaranteed 8 percent per year by simply depositing that $5 million in a bank, should the firm still build the factory? Explain using the idea of expected returns.
Explain, in one or two sentences, why a general rise in interest rates throughout the economy tends to reduce the total amount of economic investment.



Show Answer


Expected rate of return = $600,000 divided by $5,000,000 = 12 percent per year.
The factory still expected to return 12 percent, comfortably more than the guaranteed 8 percent from a bank deposit, so the firm should still build it. The factory return does carry more risk than a bank deposit, but as long as the firm believes 12 percent is the fair expected return for that risk, it remains the better choice.
Investment projects only get funded when the expected return on the project beats the return available elsewhere, such as a bank deposit or bond. When interest rates rise economy-wide, the bar an investment project has to clear rises too, so fewer projects have an expected return high enough to be worth funding, and total investment falls.

text:
Problem 3: When the Average Isn’t the Typical Household
A small country has exactly 5 households. Their annual incomes in Year 1 and Year 2 are:



Household
Year 1 Income
Year 2 Income




1
$30,000
$31,000


2
$32,000
$33,000


3
$35,000
$36,000


4
$38,000
$39,000


5
$65,000
$111,000




Compute the mean (average) household income in Year 1 and in Year 2, and the growth rate of the mean.
Compute the median household income in Year 1 and in Year 2 (the income of the middle household when incomes are sorted low to high), and the growth rate of the median.
A news report says “average income in this country grew 25 percent this year.” Is that statement misleading? Why or why not?
Relate this example back to the GDP per capita versus median household income discussion from the slides. Why might a country with healthy GDP-per-capita growth still have a lot of unhappy citizens?



Show Answer



                            
                                            



Mean, Year 1: \((30{,}000+32{,}000+35{,}000+38{,}000+65{,}000)/5 = 200{,}000/5 = \$40{,}000\). Mean, Year 2: \((31{,}000+33{,}000+36{,}000+39{,}000+111{,}000)/5 = 250{,}000/5 = \$50{,}000\). Growth rate of the mean: \((50{,}000-40{,}000)/40{,}000 = 25\) percent.
Median, Year 1 (middle of 30, 32, 35, 38, 65): $35,000. Median, Year 2 (middle of 31, 33, 36, 39, 111): $36,000. Growth rate of the median: \((36{,}000-35{,}000)/35{,}000 \approx 2.9\) percent.
It is technically true but misleading. The 25 percent figure is entirely driven by Household 5, whose income nearly doubled, while the other four households, four out of five people in this economy, saw incomes rise only about 3 percent. The “average person” implied by the mean does not resemble any actual household here.
GDP per capita is a mean, just like average income in this example. When growth is concentrated among a relatively small share of the population, GDP per capita can rise substantially even while the typical (median) household’s living standard barely improves. That gap between a healthy aggregate statistic and a stagnant typical experience is exactly the kind of thing that can make official “the economy is growing” headlines feel disconnected from how most people actually feel.

section: Problem 4: The Market for Loanable Funds
text:
Problem 4: The Market for Loanable Funds
Chapter 3 introduced supply and demand for goods, like soybeans or textbooks. The same model can describe the market where saving meets investment, called the market for loanable funds. Savers supply funds to this market (depositing money in banks, buying bonds), hoping to earn interest. Borrowers, often firms that want to invest, demand funds from this market, and have to pay interest to get them.
The table below shows the (hypothetical) market for loanable funds in a country.








Interest Rate
Quantity of Saving Supplied
Quantity of Investment Demanded

Why does it make sense to treat saving as a supply curve and investment as a demand curve in this market? What plays the role of “price”?
Using the table, what is the equilibrium interest rate, and what quantity of funds gets loaned at that rate?
Suppose the interest rate is temporarily stuck at 3 percent. Is there a shortage or surplus of loanable funds at that rate, and how large? Which direction would you expect the interest rate to move to restore equilibrium?
Using what you learned about supply and demand shifts in Chapter 3: if a new government policy encourages people to save more at every interest rate (the saving curve shifts right), what happens to the equilibrium interest rate and the equilibrium quantity of loanable funds?



Show Answer



                            
                                            



Savers act like sellers, they supply more funds to the market as the reward for doing so (the interest rate) rises, just like a seller offers more of a good as its price rises. Borrowers act like buyers, they demand fewer funds as the cost of borrowing (the interest rate) rises, just like a buyer demands less of a good as its price rises. The interest rate plays the role of price in this market.
Equilibrium interest rate is 5 percent, where quantity of saving supplied equals quantity of investment demanded, both equal $250 billion.
At 3 percent, quantity of saving supplied is $150 billion but quantity of investment demanded is $350 billion. That is a shortage of loanable funds of $200 billion, borrowers want far more funds than savers are offering at that low rate. Just like a shortage in a goods market, this pushes the interest rate up toward the \(5\) percent equilibrium, as borrowers compete for the scarce funds available.
This is exactly the same logic as a rightward supply shift in Chapter 3: more funds supplied at every interest rate pushes the equilibrium interest rate down and the equilibrium quantity of loanable funds up. Cheaper borrowing (a lower interest rate) is also exactly the kind of change that, from the investment decisions slide, would encourage firms to invest more.
